A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Clipped Density and Clipped Coverage research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, with retained material matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original metric evaluations on synthetic and image datasets, generative-model comparisons, component analyses, sensitivity tests, and computational measurements.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments and analyses, including correlations with previously collected human ratings, calibration stability, failure scenarios, and music evaluations.

M1.justification: Section 4, Equations 5–10, and Appendix B retain the same radius clipping, sample-contribution clipping, normalization, and coverage calibration procedures. Appendices J–K examine outputs without the final score cap as diagnostic variants; they do not replace the proposed metrics.

E1.justification: v3 retains the image, chest X-ray, and synthetic benchmark coverage while adding Free Music Archive data and toy time-series hallucinations in Appendix P. Appendix O adds distinct scenarios involving an absent rare real mode and incorrect within-mode correlations. The earlier distortion and Gaussian tests are retained under new appendix labels.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain Precision/Recall, Density/Coverage, symmetric and probabilistic variants, α-Precision/β-Recall, TopP&R, and Precision/Recall Cover. The new PQMass citation supplies test protocols without adding evaluated comparator results. Human ratings serve as validation criteria.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include StyleGAN truncation levels of 1.0, 0.7, and 0.5 and uncapped-score diagnostics in Appendices J–K. Appendix M introduces an ImageNet sample-size sweep from 100 to 50,000 using an 80% real/20% noise mixture. Appendices O–P add covariance, dimensionality, and signal-amplitude controls. These substantially extend the evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds human-rating validation, truncation and guidance histograms, a final-clipping ablation, calibration and sample-size analyses, rare-mode and correlation failures, and annotated FFHQ artifact inspection. These investigate perceptual agreement, metric mechanisms, stability, and failure sensitivity. Existing component, distortion, and nearest-neighbor sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 already reports means and standard deviations and discusses seed dependence. v3 adds Pearson correlations with p-values in Appendix G, specifies 100 splits for CIFAR-10 mode dropping, and explicitly identifies the music contamination experiment as single-run. The newly stated 100-split count does not establish that runs increased between versions.

E6.justification: New results include human correlations of 0.81–0.96 on three datasets but nonsignificant FFHQ correlations, and score standard deviations below 0.01 at 50,000 samples. Music Clipped Density/Coverage scores are 0.988/0.998 for balanced splits and 0.943/0.875 for genre splits. Figures 4e and 5c change α-Precision mode dropping and β-Recall matched-outlier judgments from fail to pass. Figure 22's fraction/percentage descriptions leave its minimum rare-mode detection threshold unclear.

T1.justification: The metric definitions, Lemma 1's beta-binomial expectation, calibration derivation, and Appendix A proof are unchanged. The new inverse-square-root sample-size behavior is an empirical finding, not an added asymptotic theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central claims: two outlier-robust fidelity and coverage metrics with calibration enabling linear bad-sample degradation and interpretable absolute scores. The additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Appendices J–K newly explain why truncation or guidance can initially increase both scores and produce uncapped Clipped Density above 1. Appendix I replaces v2's criticism inferred from real-data scatterplots with an explicit acknowledgment that those plots cannot establish metric superiority. Section 6 adds the absence of infinite-sample analysis, and Appendix G identifies the FFHQ human-agreement exception.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous code reference with an author-named GitHub repository and explicitly describes reproduction and metric-use access. It adds FMA preprocessing details, including middle-seven-second clips and 1024-dimensional CLAP embeddings, and documents the 2,500-sample mode-dropping exception. Appendix B's core implementation, hardware, and timing information remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Defferrard et al. (2017), Elizalde et al. (2023), Gui et al. (2024), Lemos et al. (2025), and Li et al. (2024). These support music data and embeddings, borrowed failure tests, and fidelity–coverage trade-offs. The main related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain substantively stable.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact, with localized clarifications, an expanded experimental summary, and a rewritten Appendix I interpretation. Appendices are reorganized around the additions: distortions move from G to N, toy tests from J to Q, sensitivity from K to L, and unnormalized results from L to R. Conference headers are added.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual material: human-correlation panels, truncation and guidance histograms, calibration and failure plots, modality evaluations, and real/generated sample grids with FFHQ defect annotations. Existing plots receive larger, differentiated markers and revised axes or legends, and several appendix figures move. Tables 1–8 retain their structure.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's lack of direct human-rating validation and dedicated quantification of absolute-score variability with sample size through Figure 8 and Figures 19–20. Appendices J–K clarify clipping behavior, while Appendix I removes unsupported conclusions from real-data scatterplots. Together these strengthen evidence and interpretation for the central claims. Nonsignificant FFHQ correlations, single-run music results, and Figure 22's percentage ambiguity limit the added support but do not outweigh these gains.
